headline: New build demand constrained by price points of $750k–$800k and higher holding costs during construction as rates rise
reasoning: Palash Dave notes that clients are attracted to new builds primarily for tax benefits such as depreciation, but the entry price for a house-and-land package in any decent area is typically $750,000–$800,000, which is beyond the borrowing capacity of most prospective buyers. Additionally, buyers face the risk that interest rates rise further during the construction period, increasing out-of-pocket holding costs before the property generates any rental income. This combination of high price points and elevated construction-period risk is dampening new build demand despite government budget measures aimed at boosting supply.
quote: The clients which are coming to us or what is happening is they are definitely more inclined towards buying a brand new property predominantly because of the tax benefits. They see the challenge is the pricing for the brand new build in any decent area is not less than 700 eight $800,000... they don't have the capacity or the boring ability to do and go do that purchase. They're also hesitant right now that the holding period, by the time the property, the land is purchased and the property is built, the interest rate is higher. So they have to fork out a lot more from their pocket to actually get to the point where the property is going to start getting some rent.
episode_title: Housing hits pause as buyers back off

headline: Upgraders with borrowing capacity have a strong opportunity now: selling a discounted asset to buy a more discounted, higher-value one
reasoning: Palash Dave argues that the current soft market creates a compelling asymmetric opportunity for property upgraders. If a $2 million property falls 10% the seller loses $200,000, but the $4 million property they are buying into has likely also fallen by a similar percentage, meaning the net saving on the upgrade is far larger in dollar terms. For those who have the borrowing capacity, this represents a lifestyle and financial upgrade at better-than-expected prices compared to a year ago.
quote: I think it's a very good time only because you've got you're selling a property which is probably cheaper. Let's say you have a property, your own property of $2,000,000 for example. And if it falls by, you know, let's say 10%, which lot of places it has, you're losing only 200,000, but you're buying a property with let's say $4 million. And if that is also, you know, that is something you can get into and you can afford to, you can make that lifestyle change. So a lot of people are trying to get the benefit of getting into an upgraded property then what they were, what they would have planned even a year back or so. And I guess that's the opportunity, people who have have the borrowing capacity for them. It's a great opportunity in my view.
episode_title: Housing hits pause as buyers back off

headline: Buyers frozen in a 'checkmate' situation as rising rates, inflation uncertainty and tax changes weigh on sentiment across the entire property ecosystem
reasoning: Palash Dave argues that a combination of higher interest rates (which compress borrowing capacity), uncertainty around RBA decisions and upcoming October inflation data, and tax policy changes have created a stalemate in the Australian residential property market. The paralysis extends beyond buyers and sellers to ancillary professionals such as solicitors, building inspectors, cleaners, and removalists who are all reporting reduced workloads. He believes the market will remain on hold until consumer sentiment improves and there is greater macro clarity, particularly around the Christmas period.
quote: What we are very conscious right now is the number of people who are just waiting and holding for this cycle to finish or at least have some clarity. I think we've had a lot of information about interest rates, the tax changes and all the things which are happening in the Australian economy and outside the world, which is just holding people back. So unless until we get some clarity and the consumer sentiment improves, I think we just, you know, sort of a checkmate situation right now, we're just holding on. Everybody's just kind of worried. And not only the buyers and the sellers, but everybody around that whole setup, which is, you know, your solicitors, your build and best inspection guys, your professional cleaners, the removalists, they're all worried and they're, they don't have as much to do as what they used to have a few months back.
episode_title: Housing hits pause as buyers back off

headline: First home buyers and first-time investors have effectively exited the market; only experienced investors and upgraders remain active
reasoning: Palash Dave observes that open house attendance across the three major states has dropped dramatically, with roughly two or three people visiting across a typical agent's six listed properties. First-time investors have completely stopped entering the market and first home buyer numbers have also dropped sharply. The most active cohort is existing homeowners upgrading by leveraging accumulated equity. Experienced investors are still present but cautious. First home buyers are choosing to stay with family given the combination of high rates, high prices, and insufficient borrowing power.
quote: There is definitely a lot lower number of people walking into open houses. So I'm speaking to our agents who we work with in all let's say the three major states. And if I was to put out an average, if in a good agent will have about 6 properties in the market where they're going open houses, there will be approximately two or three people walking into the combination of 6 properties. So that's a extremely low number... The experienced investor is still there, the first time investor is gone and also the first one buyers. Their number have drastically dropped as well.

headline: Each 25bp rate hike strips roughly $12,000–$24,000 from household borrowing capacity; four hikes this year have wiped ~$100,000, with property prices not falling fast enough to compensate
reasoning: Palash Dave explains that each 25bp RBA rate increase reduces borrowing capacity by approximately $12,000–$24,000 per household. With four hikes already in the current year, around $100,000 of borrowing capacity has been eroded for a typical dual-income household. Despite this, property prices are not falling quickly enough to offset the lost capacity, making purchases increasingly unaffordable. Banks are also assessing borrowers on a 3% serviceability buffer above the offered rate, meaning assessment occurs at around 9.6% in the current environment, further restricting pre-approvals.
quote: So you're right both in, in this year itself and 25 basis points normally equates to anywhere from about 12,000 to $24,000 shaved off your borrowing capacity. So in a year we've already had four, it's just around 100,000 wiped off a normal household with two incomes, another one, another 25, let's say 25,000 off. If you have $125,000 of borrowing capacity stripped off a household, the property pricing is not falling as quickly.
